title: Turnkey Construction or Labor-Only Contract: Pros and Cons Compared
desc: Turnkey or labor-only, buying materials yourself? Compare cost, risk, homeowner responsibility and warranty, and how to choose what suits your family.
summary: Compares two common ways to build a house – turnkey and labor-only with self-purchased materials – on cost, effort, risk, responsibility and warranty.
body: p

When building a house, homeowners usually choose one of two approaches: turnkey (the contractor provides both materials and labor) or labor-only (the homeowner buys the materials and only hires workers). Each has its own pros and cons; choosing wrongly easily costs money or causes months of exhaustion.
h2
1. How do the two approaches differ?
ul

Turnkey: a construction contract in which the contractor builds according to the design and may supply materials and equipment for construction (Point b, Clause 2, Article 8 of Decree 210/2026/ND-CP); the price is fixed at signing and corresponds to the scope of work (Point a, Clause 2, Article 6).

Labor-only: the homeowner buys the materials and pays wages to a team of workers. Either way, a written contract should be made, clearly stating the work, quality, price, payment, deadlines and liability for breach (Article 398 of the Civil Code).
h2
2. The homeowner's responsibility: it cannot all be “contracted out”
p

For a detached house, the house owner organizes construction and supervision and is responsible for safety in construction, for the safety of adjacent buildings and for the environment (Point b, Clause 3, Article 10 of Decree 207/2026/ND-CP). The items to be supervised include construction methods, the quality of materials before they are used, scaffolding, temporary supports and safety measures (Clause 4, Article 10). With labor-only, where the homeowner buys the materials, the homeowner directly bears responsibility for material quality.
h2
3. Quick comparison
ul
Cost: labor-only can be cheaper because the homeowner chooses where to buy and pays no management fee or profit on materials; turnkey is easier to budget because the price is fixed from the start.
Effort: labor-only requires the homeowner to have time to order materials on time, count them and store them; turnkey is less work.
Risk of loss and late materials: labor-only – borne by the homeowner; turnkey – borne by the contractor within the scope of the contract.
Extra costs: in turnkey they arise when the scope is unclear; in labor-only they arise when the homeowner buys too little, too much or changes their mind.
Quality disputes: turnkey – responsibility is concentrated in one party; labor-only – it is hard to tell whether the fault lies with the materials or the workers.
h2
4. How does the warranty differ?
p

Organizations and individuals that build housing must give a warranty; a detached house has a warranty of at least 24 months from completion and acceptance for use (Clauses 1 and 2, Article 129 of the Housing Law). For equipment, the warranty follows the manufacturer's term. With labor-only, where the homeowner buys the materials, the homeowner deals directly with the seller or manufacturer – keep invoices and warranty cards. For details see Warranty for houses and construction works.
h2
5. Which should you choose?
ul
Choose turnkey if the family is busy, not familiar with materials, wants a fixed budget and one party responsible – but read the scope of the quote carefully.
Choose labor-only if a family member is knowledgeable, has time to follow the site daily, and the house is small.
The hybrid approach: turnkey for the rough structure, with the homeowner choosing and buying the finishing materials (tiles, sanitary fixtures, lamps) at an agreed ceiling unit price.
p

Whichever you choose, the work crew must have sufficient capability for the scale of the building – see Penalties for building contrary to the design or hiring workers without sufficient capability. If you need advice on a suitable option, you can contact Quan Construction.
